title: Selectivity regulation of CO2 electroreduction through contact interface engineering on superwetting Cu nanoarray electrodes
abstract: Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction is a promising way to mitigate the urgent energy and environmental issues, but how to increase the selectivity for desired product among multiple competing reaction pathways remains a bottleneck. Here, we demonstrate that engineering the gas–liquid–solid contact interface on the electrode surface could tailor the selectivity of CO2 reduction and meanwhile suppress H2 production through regulated reaction kinetics. Specifically, polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) was utilized to modify a Cu nanoarray electrode as an example, which is able to change the electrode surface from aerophobic to aerophilic state. The enriched nano-tunnels of the Cu nanoarray electrode can facilitate CO2 transportation and pin gaseous products on the electrode surface. The latter is believed to be the reason that boosts the Faradaic efficiency of liquid products by 67% and limits the H2 production to less than half of before. This interface engineering strategy also lowered H2O (proton) affinity, therefore promoting CO and HCOOH production. Engineering the electrode contact interface controls the reaction kinetics and the selectivity of products, which should be inspiring for other electrochemical reactions.

sections.text: KEYWORDS CO2 reduction, selectivity, copper, contact interface, reaction kinetics

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
With the over-consumption of fossil fuels and excessive accumulation of CO2 greenhouse gas in the atmosphere, the catalytic electroreduction of CO2 to fuels and value-added chemicals becomes one of the most important energy and environmental challenges [1–7]. Electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) consists of multistep electron/proton transfer processes and multiple pathways, resulting in sluggish reaction kinetics and a wide distribution of reduction products. On this subject, many active electrocatalysts (e.g. Au, Cu, Sn, etc.) have been identified to promote the reaction kinetics [8–14]. Over the past decade, Cu material has received special interests to pursue distinctive CO2RR performance due to the suitable adsorption/ desorption ability of various intermediates for value-added hydrocarbon products [15–20]. But the selectivity is still a big issue so far. Besides, the side reaction (i.e. hydrogen evolution reaction, HER) always competes with CO2RR in the working potential range, leading to a low efficiency/poor selectivity of carbonaceous product. A number of strategies including size- and shape-control [21, 22], alloying [23, 24], and introducing grain boundaries [25, 26] have been developed to improve the intrinsic activity/selectivity, but limited success has been achieved so far. Therefore, exploring new strategy to simultaneously improve the carbonaceous product selectivity and
suppress the side reaction is still a significant challenge. Generally, the electrocatalytic performance of an electrode depends on several factors including: 1) the chemical nature of the material that is in direct relation to the intrinsic property of the active sites [27–29]; 2) the accessibility of the reactive components for the electrochemical reactions, governed by the electrode architecture [30–32]; and 3) the conductivity and structural integrity of the catalyst to permit efficient electron transmission [33]. Nanowire (NW) array, which can be achieved by in situ cultivating on conductive supports, represents a highly oriented nanostructure with controllable dimensions. It shows a potential for high-performance electrodes, as it could offer increased specific surface areas for electrochemical reactions, and reduce the aggregation of active sites, as well as afford highways for mass and electron transport. As a typical example, Smith’s group recently reported Cu NW arrays for electrocatalytic CO2 reduction, the selectivity could be tuned by systematically altering length and density of the Cu NWs [34]. However, CO2RR is a typical gas involved reaction, gas–liquid–solid contact interface would influence the reaction kinetics and consequently control the selectivity. The deep understanding on this effect is still a key missing piece for the performance optimization of an electrode.
From our point of view, constructing three-dimensional (3D) array electrode could not only enhance mass and electron transfer to

improve the CO2 reduction activity, but also facilitate the competing HER, leading to limited improvement of CO2RR efficiency [35–37]. Things turn clearer when it is noticed that CO2RR is a gas-consuption reaction, while HER is a gas-evolution reaction. It is thus deductive that a “bubble-pinning” system would favorite the former by providing a surface CO2-enriched local microenvironment but suppress the latter by keeping more H2 products. And such engineering on the interface, if balancing the gas, ion diffusion and electron transfer, would tailor the reaction pathways and products at the same time.
Herein, as a proof-of-concept demonstration, we report the first study of CO2RR kinetics/selectivity control on highly dense Cu NW array electrode by engineering the contact interface. The as-prepared Cu catalyst showed an aerophilic surface (Fig. 1) after surface modification with polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE), which behaved distinctly different toward the gas/liquid diffusion than before. As a result, the PTFE-Cu electrode exhibits enhanced CO2RR and suppressed HER at the same time. The liquid production is facilitated, and the gas generation is suppressed on the aerophilic Cu electrode. Besides, engineering the contact interface regulated the reaction kinetics, leading to HCOOH and CO dominated products.

sections.heading: 2.1 Preparation of aerophilic Cu array electrode
sections.text: The synthesis of PTFE-Cu NW array involves a chemical deposition method to prepare Cu NW array and a coating of PTFE on the array surface. Specifically, a Cu foil was cleaned ultrasonically in acetone/ ethanol and rinsed with deionized water. Then, the cleaned Cu foil was dried with nitrogen and immersed into a mixed solution containing 0.13 M (NH4)2S2O8 and 2.66 M NaOH for 10 min. The deep-blue color foil (Cu(OH)2 NW array formed on the surface of the foil) was taken out from the solution, rinsed with deionized water/ethanol. To coat PTFE on the array surface, the as-prepared Cu(OH)2 NW array was soaked in PTFE solution (1 wt.%, 5 wt.%, 10 wt.%, and 20 wt.%) for 10 min, then annealed at 350 °C for 30 min under an air atmosphere, forming PTFE-CuO NW array. The subsequent reducing procedure is conducted at –0.7 V vs. RHE in 0.1 M KHCO3 for 10 min to reduce PTEF-CuO to PTFE-Cu. As a comparison, pristine Cu NW array was made following the same procedures but without coating with PTFE.

sections.heading: 2.2 Structural characterizations
sections.text: The morphologies of as-synthesized samples were characterized by field-emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (JEOL JSM6335, 20 kV) and high-solution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) (JEOL, JEM-2100, 200 kV). X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were collected on Shimadzu XRD-6000 with Cu Kα radiation (40 kV, 30 mA, λ = 1.5418 Å), recorded with 2θ ranging from 10° to 80°. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) measurements were carried out with a PHI Quantera II XPS Scanning Microprobe. The bubble and drop contact angles were measured by the optical contact angle measurement (Dataphysics OCA20) in ambient air at room temperature. The volume of the gas bubble and liquid drop was ~ 2 and 1 μL, respectively. All experiments were repeated at least 5 times.

sections.heading: 2.3 Electrochemical measurements
sections.text: The electrochemical measurements were carried out using a BioLogic VMP3 electrochemistry workstation. A homemade gas-tight H-type electrochemical cell separated by a cation exchange membrane (Nafion N115, DuPont) was used. The electrolyte was 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution which had been electrochemically purified for 24 h before use. The CO2 gas flow rate was 20 sccm. The working electrode was the as-prepared Cu electrode with an active area of 0.2 cm2. A graphite rod was used as the counter electrode and an Ag/AgCl electrode was used as the reference electrode. The reference electrode was periodically calibrated, and the potential applied on the working electrode was corrected using the IR compensation function of the electrochemistry workstation.

sections.heading: 3 Results and discussion
sections.text:
The superaerophobic Cu NW array electrode was prepared by a chemical deposition procedure. Namely, Cu(OH)2 NWs were firstly grown on Cu foil substrate. After annealing at 350 °C, the Cu(OH)2 turned to CuO, as confirmed by the change of XRD patterns before and after annealling (Fig. S1 in the Electronic Supplementary Material (ESM)). The subsequent electrochemical reduction led to the formation of metallic Cu array, as evidenced by both XPS and XRD characterizations (Figs. S1 and S2 in the ESM). The SEM image confirmed the morphology of NW array after electrochemical reduction (Fig. 2(a)). The width of the nanowire was ~ 100 nm as revealed by TEM characterization of a single Cu wire peeled off from the array electrode (Fig. 2(b)). HRTEM showed obvious grain boundaries on the surface of Cu nanowire, suggesting polycrystalline nature of Cu NW (Fig. 2(c)) and the selected area electron diffraction results further confirmed its polycrystalline feature (Fig. S3 in the ESM). The electrode assembled by arrayed Cu NWs showed a superaerophobic surface, as evidenced by a contact angle of 154.4° for CO2 gas bubbles on such a Cu array surface (Fig. 2(d)). Meanwhile, the contact angle for the 0.1 M KHCO3 aqueous solution (i.e. CO2RR electrolyte) was 32.9°, revealing a hydrophilic state. This aerophobic surface nature facilitated the leaving of gas products thus giving a stable current density (Fig. 2(e)). However, when immersing the Cu NW array electrode in a 5% PTFE solution, a thin layer of PTFE was uniformly coated on the surface of Cu NWs (Fig. 2(b) and Fig. S4 in the ESM), which changed the affinity towards gaseous CO2 and electrolyte significantly (Fig. 2(f)). Meanwhile, both the Cu NW array structure and the surface electronic structure were maintained (Figs. S5 and S6 in the ESM). The contact angles for CO2 gas bubbles and electrolytes were measured to be 48.4° and 136.6°, respectively, suggesting the surface turned from aerophobic/hydrohpilic to aerophilic/hydrophobic state. Such a gas affinitive surface would lead to a stronger bubble adhesion, and hold the gaseous products for a longer time during electrochemical CO2RR process. Thus, the bubbles were kept on the electrode surface till the size got bigger than 1 mm or more. When the size of product bubbles got large

The CO2RR performances of the as-prepared aerophobic and aerophillic Cu electrodes were tested in CO2-saturated 0.1 M KHCO3(aq) electrolyte to investigate the catalytic selectivity change induced by the gas/liquid/solid contact interface difference. Without PTFE modification, the pristine Cu array showed a Faraday efficiency (FE) of ~ 40% for H2 production and FE of ~ 60% for carbonaceous products, and gas products were in dominance over the whole potential range (Fig. 3(a)). In a more negative potential range, hydrocarbon products were more favorable than CO. This performance was in consistent with the Cu NW array electrode reported previously [34]. After PTFE modification, the current density under different working potentials did not change so much but the product distribution was largely different (Figs. 3(b) and 3(c)). Under all working potentials, the FEs of H2 were restrained to < 20%, less than half of the value observed on the pristine Cu array electrode. Besides, the FEs of liquid products were enhanced and the FEs of gas products from CO2RR were suppressed at the same time. In more negative potential range, C1 products including CO and HCOOH were greatly facilitated. Such enhanced selectivity was attributed to the contact interface engineering that changed the electrode surface to aerophilic/hydrophobic state, which drove the liquid products off the catalyst surface easily but restricted the gaseous products from releasing. In addition, the hydrophobic nature of the electrode surface also altered the catalytic kinetics by restraining proton supply from the aqueous electrolyte to the catalyst surface. More direct evidence came from the HER behavior of PTFE-modified Cu array electrode (Fig. S7 in the ESM). The Tafel slope of pristine Cu array was 116 mV/dec, demonstrating proton adsorption (i.e. Volmer reaction) was the rate-determining step [38]. Notably, the greater Tafel slope of PTFE-modified Cu array (131 mV/dec) suggested the hindered proton adsorption from the electrolyte. Moreover, for the PTFE-modified Cu array, the supply
of a CO2 gas bubble upon the electrode surface would lead to the drastic increase of current (Fig. S8 in the ESM), demonstrating the critical role of an aerophilic surface on providing a CO2-enrich local microenvironment to enhance CO2RR, although the CO2 feedstock source during electrocatalysis (supplied CO2 gas or dissolved CO2 molecules) is still under investigation [39]. Taking the hindered proton adsorption and the CO2-enrich local microenvironment together, the HER process was suppressed and CO2RR reaction pathways with fewer hydrogen involving was facilitated (i.e. CO and HCOOH generation, Table S1 in the ESM) [40].
Cu array electrodes immersed in PTFE solutions with different concentrations (1%–20%) were prepared to further identify the selectivity change through contact interface engineering. As a result, increasing PTFE concentration (up to 5%) obviously increased the CO2RR current density though the ECSA of the electrode decreased slightly, demonstrating the enhanced electrocatalytic activity towards CO2RR (Fig. 3(d), and Fig. S9 and Table S2 in the ESM). This implied the CO2RR was controlled by both CO2 and electrolytes supply, and slightly surface modification could facilitate the balancing between CO2 absorption and proton supply. However, with the concentration of PTFE going even higher (5%–20%), the current density for CO2RR dropped quickly (Fig. S10 in the ESM), because the active sites were covered by excessive PTFE molecules. Current optimization thus suggested that 5% PTFE is enough. Besides, the Cu array electrode

modified with different concentrations of PTFE showed almost the same solution resistance (Fig. S11 in the ESM), suggesting that the electrical conductivity change upon PTFE modification is negligible.
As to the product distribution, it was clearly observed that HER was suppressed and CO2RR was facilitated upon PTFE modification (Fig. 3(e)), and FE of liquid products increased greatly while gas production was restrained (Fig. 3(f)). But it should be noted that such selectivity changes only happened in the concentration range of 1%–5%. Higher PTFE concentration would not further enhance the selectivity, suggesting that 5% PTFE has endowed enough aerophilicity to the surface and more PTFE would not change the surface wettability a lot but would cover too many active sites. For detailed product distribution (Fig. 3(g)), CO was greatly facilitated among all gas products while hydrocarbon products were suppressed. This was due to the limited proton supply on the hydrophobic PTFE-Cu surface. Similar suppression effects on H-containing liquid products were also observed (Fig. 3(h)), where the production of HCOOH was largely enhanced but that of C2+C3 liquid products (ethanol and n-propanol) was suppressed, further suggesting the hydrophobic surface effect (Fig. S10 in the ESM).
The contact angles of CO2RR products were measured to get deeper insight into the CO2RR selectivity change upon affinity modulation. The pristine Cu array electrode showed a superaerophobic surface for all gas products including H2, CO, and C2H4 (~ 150°, Fig. 4(a)). After PTFE modification, the electrode surface turned into aerophilic for H2 (66.7°) and C2H4 (86.8°), suggesting a holding effect for these gas products, thus slowing down H2 and C2H4 formation kinetics. Surprisingly, the contact angle of CO on PTFE-Cu array was 104.3°, suggesting strong aerophobicity, which was conducive for CO product desorption, thus boosting CO production. Besides, considering that CO production needs the least amount of protons as compared with other products, CO formation was kinetically favorable on a hydrophobic surface which hindered proton supply from the electrolyte. Taking together of the limited proton supply and the enhanced desorption behavior, the FE of CO increased (by 60%) on the PTFE-modified Cu array electrode.
Similar trend was found on liquid products. After contact interface engineering, the electrode surface changed from hydrophilic to hydrophobic towards HCOOH, thus the CO2RR pathway to formic acid was kinetically facilitated (Fig. 4(c)). However, the wettabilities towards ethanol and n-propanol did not change so much, leading to tiny variation on their FEs. When plotting the FE change (ΔFE) upon the surface contact angle change (Δθ) for various products (Figs. 4(b) and 4(d)), it was found that the two variables were positively relative, i.e. large contact angle change resulted in large FE change,
demonstrating the contact interface engineering method as an efficient strategy to control the CO2RR selectivity.

sections.heading: 4 Conclusion
sections.text: In summary, we report that engineering the contact interface on superwetting Cu electrode could control CO2RR selectivity. Upon optimized PTFE modification, the CO2 adsorption was promoted and the proton supply was limited, leading to the enhanced H-depleted C1 (i.e. CO/HCOOH) production and suppressed side HER, thus altering the product distribution. This work demonstrates engineering the contact interface as an effective way to control the intrinsic activity/selectivity of an electrode, emphasizes the importance of reagents diffusion on catalytic selectivity for a multi-pathway reaction, and should be inspiring for advanced electrodes design towards CO2RR and other reaction systems.
